implementation_notes: Rails' recommended form makes the link table a model: the join model belongs_to both ends, the two sides declare has_many :through, and because the join table is a real Active Record model the association can carry columns, validations and callbacks. ActiveRecord inserts and deletes the join rows as records are created or destroyed, which is Association Table Mapping with an explicit association entity. Rails documents this as the form to prefer over has_and_belongs_to_many precisely because the association is expected to grow.
code_sketch:
class FilmActor < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :actor
  belongs_to :film
  validates :actor_id, uniqueness: { scope: :film_id }
end

class Actor < ApplicationRecord
  has_many :film_actors, dependent: :destroy
  has_many :films, through: :film_actors
end

actor.films << film          # creates the join row
pitfalls: Without a unique index (or uniqueness validation) on the pair, << can insert the same association twice.
dependent: :destroy on the join association destroys join rows one by one; :delete_all skips callbacks - pick deliberately, because both are needed for clean deletion.
The join model does not prevent two writers: both sides can create the same link unless uniqueness is enforced in the database.

variants.name: has_and_belongs_to_many over an implicit join table
variants.implementation_notes: has_and_belongs_to_many declares the many-to-many with no intervening model: Rails expects a join table named from the two table names in alphabetical order, with two foreign-key columns and no id column, and manages the link rows through the collection API. It is the leanest declaration of the pattern and the reason Rails docs warn against it - no model means no payload, no validations and no callbacks on the association, so the table must stay purely a pair list.
variants.code_sketch:
class Actor < ApplicationRecord
  has_and_belongs_to_many :films
end

class Film < ApplicationRecord
  has_and_belongs_to_many :actors
end

# join table: actors_films (alphabetical), columns actor_id, film_id, no id column
actor.films << film          # INSERT INTO actors_films
actor.films.destroy(film)    # DELETE FROM actors_films
pitfalls: The join table must carry no primary key of its own and Rails derives its name alphabetically from the two table names: a hand-created table with a surrogate id and no unique index accepts duplicate links silently.
No unique constraint is implied on the pair, so << repeated creates duplicate links.
There is no join model, so the association cannot grow payload columns later without a migration to has_many :through.
destroy on the collection deletes only the link row, which is usually what you want but surprises readers expecting the record to go.
variants.idiom_name: has_and_belongs_to_many over an implicit join table
